Understanding Stocks, ETFs & Securities

Illustration for understanding stocks, etfs & securities.

Illustration for understanding stocks, etfs & securities.

A stock is an ownership interest in a company. A new share issue can raise money for the issuer; buying existing shares in the secondary market normally pays the selling holder. Ownership does not promise dividends or a higher resale price.

💡
Example

Hypothetical share arithmetic: 10 shares at $200 cost $2,000 before fees. At $250 they are worth $2,500, a $500 unrealized gain before costs; at $150 they are worth $1,500, a $500 loss. Market capitalization is price times shares outstanding: 2 billion shares at $50 gives $100 billion. These are invented inputs, not current company valuations.

An ETF is a fund structure, not a risk rating

An exchange-traded fund gives the exposure specified by its mandate and holdings. A broad equity index fund and a concentrated or leveraged single-stock fund have very different risks. The ETF label alone does not establish diversification, low volatility or suitability.

Read the objective, holdings, concentration, expense ratio and any leverage or daily-reset terms in current fund documents.
SPY and QQQ follow different indexes; QQQ is not a fund containing only technology companies. Fund holdings can overlap with shares already held.
Other products include issuer debt, commodity exposures and derivative contracts. Their legal rights, costs and settlement terms differ.
💡
Example

Compare an invented two-company fund holding 50% in each name with a single-company holding. If one share falls 20% and the other is unchanged, the equally weighted fund falls 10% before costs. If both fall 20%, the fund also falls 20%: multiple holdings do not eliminate market losses.

Pro Tip

In TradeHQ, inspect the selected practice instrument and quote label before entering a market order. Options and futures lessons explain contracts conceptually; the simulator does not execute those contracts.

How to Read Stock Quotes & Charts

Illustration for how to read stock quotes & charts.

A quote is an observation from a source at a time, not a guarantee of the next execution price. Check currency, timestamp, bid, ask and whether data are delayed or generated. Last price, bid and ask answer different questions.

Bid: a quoted price at which a participant is willing to buy; ask: a quoted selling price. Available size and routing affect execution.
Last price: the most recently reported transaction in the displayed feed. It can differ from both current quotes.
Volume: units traded in a specified interval. A chart must identify the interval and venue or coverage.
💡
Example

An invented bid of $99.90 and ask of $100.10 have a $0.20 spread. A displayed last trade of $100 is not a promise that a new purchase will fill there. Ten shares bought at $100.10 and immediately sold at $99.90 lose $2 before any fees, assuming both quotes fill.

Read the interval before the shape

A line chart connects a chosen series such as closing prices. A candle records open, high, low and close for an interval. Under the common green-up convention, a green body means close above open; color settings can differ. Neither color nor body length predicts the next candle.

💡
Example

For a candle with open 100, high 105, low 99 and close 103, the body spans 3 and the full range spans 6. A daily candle and a one-minute candle can have that same shape while representing different observations.

Pro Tip

TradeHQ charts may use provider data or generated practice series, as labeled. Generated candles are illustrations and cannot establish actual past market behavior.

Market Orders vs. Limit Orders

Order types describe different trade-offs between execution and price control. This lesson explains their mechanics rather than recommending one order type for every situation.

Market Orders: Execution Before Price Control

A market order seeks to buy or sell promptly at available prices. The last quoted price may differ from the fill price, particularly in fast or thin markets. Trading halts and limited liquidity can interrupt execution.

💡
Example

Hypothetical example: a quote shows $200 and an order requests 10 shares. A $200.50 fill costs $2,005 before fees, while a $199.50 fill costs $1,995. The quote alone does not establish the final cost.

Limit Orders: A Price Condition

A buy limit specifies the highest acceptable purchase price; a sell limit specifies the lowest acceptable sale price. Execution is at that price or better, but the order may fill only partly or not at all. Reaching the limit does not guarantee a fill because other orders may have priority.

💡
Example

A hypothetical buy limit at $195 cannot fill above $195. If the market stays higher, the order remains unfilled. Even if a fill occurs, the asset can subsequently fall in value.

Stop and Stop-Limit Mechanics

A stop order becomes a market order when its trigger is reached. A stop-limit instead becomes a limit order. A stop can execute beyond its trigger after a gap; a stop-limit can remain unfilled. Neither guarantees a maximum loss.

What TradeHQ Supports

TradeHQ executes simulated market orders. It does not place resting limit, stop or trailing-stop orders. Study those mechanics using a worksheet; recording an exit condition does not automate it in the simulator.

Pro Tip

For a worksheet exercise, compare a market-order fill with an unfilled limit-order case and a stop triggered after a price gap. Record the assumptions, fees and remaining exposure rather than assuming any order type is always preferable.

Reference

SEC Investor.gov — Types of Orders and Stop, Stop-Limit, and Trailing Stop Orders explain the execution trade-offs: https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/how-stock-markets-work/types-orders and https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/general-resources/news-alerts/alerts-bulletins/investor-bulletins-15

Trading Hours & Market Sessions

Trading schedules belong to a venue and product. For regular Nasdaq stock trading, the scheduled session is 9:30 a.m.–4 p.m. Eastern Time on business days, subject to holidays, early closes and interruptions. Eastern Time changes its UTC offset seasonally.

Nasdaq currently defines pre-market as 4:00–9:30 a.m. Eastern and post-market as 4:00–8:00 p.m. Eastern. Access, eligible orders and broker rules vary.
An exchange schedule does not guarantee liquidity, stable prices or a fill. Spreads and available size can differ outside the regular session.
Many crypto venues ordinarily operate continuously, but maintenance, outages and product restrictions can interrupt access. A continuously open venue does not establish a predictable weekend return.
💡
Example

If an exchange is open at 10 a.m. Eastern, a broker may still restrict a particular product or order. Record the venue, date and time zone instead of assuming that every stock, fund, currency pair and token shares one schedule.

Pro Tip

The TradeHQ practice engine is not an exchange-hours enforcement service. A simulated fill outside a real venue session does not prove a real order could execute then. Check the relevant venue and broker rules for actual activity.
